clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant axonal (type 2) Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease caused by heterozygous mutations in AARS1, encoding cytoplasmic alanyl-tRNA synthetase.
One of the aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase (ARS) neuropathies, a family that also includes GARS1 (CMT2D) and YARS1 (dominant intermediate CMT type C).
Typical length-dependent picture: distal lower-limb weakness, pes cavus, hammer toes and distal sensory loss, usually with late-adolescent or adult onset.
Nerve conduction studies show an axonal pattern, with reduced motor and sensory amplitudes but relatively preserved conduction velocities.
Both motor and sensory fibres are involved, which helps separate it from the purely motor phenotypes seen with some other synthetase genes.
Progression is characteristically slow, with the hands affected after the legs in a length-dependent sequence.
Diagnosis rests on identifying a pathogenic AARS1 variant on a neuropathy gene panel or exome study in a patient with axonal CMT and a compatible pedigree.
Variable expressivity and reduced penetrance are common within affected families.
reference.pathophysiology: AARS1 encodes cytoplasmic alanyl-tRNA synthetase, one of the aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases that charge transfer RNA with its cognate amino acid, here alanine, during protein translation. Heterozygous, usually missense, mutations impair aminoacylation and the enzyme's proofreading function that normally prevents mischarging of tRNA. The resulting reduction in functional enzyme, together with possible dominant-negative or toxic effects on the obligate dimeric protein, is thought to render long peripheral axons, which depend on brisk local protein synthesis, selectively vulnerable, producing a length-dependent axonal degeneration. Why a ubiquitously expressed housekeeping enzyme causes an axon-restricted phenotype remains incompletely understood, a recurring theme across the ARS-related neuropathies.
additionalDifferentials: CMT2D (GARS1) and other ARS-related neuropathies (YARS1, HARS1, WARS1, MARS1, KARS1)
CMT2A (MFN2) and other autosomal dominant axonal CMT subtypes
Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies when the presentation appears patchy
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to confirm the axonal pattern
Targeted CMT/neuropathy gene panel or exome sequencing that includes AARS1
Family segregation testing and detailed pedigree analysis
Clinical genetics referral and genetic counselling
Screening for acquired causes of axonal neuropathy before attributing symptoms to the variant
Assessment of foot deformity and gait with orthopaedic or podiatry input
redFlags: Rapid or markedly asymmetric progression suggesting a superimposed acquired neuropathy
Prominent proximal weakness or bulbar or respiratory involvement, which is atypical and prompts reappraisal
Sensory ataxia or florid positive sensory symptoms out of keeping with slow axonal CMT
reference.prognosis: CMT2N usually follows a slowly progressive course with ambulation preserved for many years and normal life expectancy, although distal weakness and foot deformity can cause increasing disability over decades.
pitfalls: Assuming that preserved conduction velocities exclude CMT, when reduced amplitudes are the key axonal marker.
Overlooking the ARS group so that AARS1 is not included on the chosen gene panel.
Attributing a treatable intercurrent acquired neuropathy to the inherited disorder.
Expecting a single uniform phenotype despite the variable expressivity and reduced penetrance typical of ARS mutations.
